title: ‘This word is God’s’ rests on moral evidence that should remove doubt
source_text: XXXVII. Ac profecto judicium illud, quo mens nostra statuit verbum ac testimonium, quod proponitur ipsi ut credendorum argumentum, vere divinum esse, non nascitur quidem ex tali perceptione, qualis est illa qua intellectus noster admittit lucem innatam primorum principiorum, & veritatem propositionum quae necessario ex iis deducuntur: sed tamen fundatur in argumentis, notis & indiciis, quae moraliter saltem, evidens reddunt rem ita se habere, adeoque possunt, ac debent ex mente bene affecta tollere omnem dubitationem, & illam certam & securam reddere.
pass_a_gloss: And indeed that judgment by which our mind lays down that the word and testimony proposed to it as the argument of things to be believed is truly divine is not born from such a perception as that by which our intellect admits the innate light of first principles and the truth of propositions necessarily deduced from them: yet it is founded on arguments, marks, and indications which at least morally make evident that the thing so stands, and therefore can and ought from a well-affected mind to take away every doubt and render it certain and secure.
pass_b_english: Still founded on moral marks/arguments that make the matter evident.
Can/ought to clear all doubt in a well-affected mind.

lemmas.gloss: it is founded on arguments, marks, and indications

choices.term: possunt, ac debent ex mente bene affecta tollere omnem dubitationem
choices.english: can and ought from a well-affected mind to take away every doubt
choices.why: Moral grounds still ought to secure the mind.
rejected: moral marks cannot remove doubt at all
